highlights.text: qisma ḍīzā ("a ḍīzā division/share"): a deficient apportionment, i.e. a share that shortchanges someone
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's core sense of the root

highlights.text: "so your right is denied [maḍʾūz], and your nose is humbled"
highlights.note: unattributed verse (the entry names no poet)

highlights.text: two sound bases: (I) a specific number — "ten" — which is then extended to other things, and (II) mingling and entering-into
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's two origins for the root

highlights.text: عَشَرَة "ten" (masc.), عَشْر (fem.).
عَشِير = one who associates with you
عَشِيرَة (kin-group) is so named from members' mutual association; even a husband is his wife's عَشِير
الْمَعْشَر = any group united in one affair
(Shāhid: Zuhayr, on long companionship breeding weariness.)
Imruʾ al-Qays: "the shattered pieces — أَعْشَار — of a slain heart"
a hadith about women: "you curse much and are ungrateful to the ʿashīr [companion/husband]"
highlights.note: a hadith, used for the sense of ʿashīr

highlights.text: a single sound root meaning darkness and lack of clarity in a thing
ʿishāʾ — the first darkness of nightfall
al-ʿashiyy — the end of the day (late afternoon/evening)
Zuhayr's famous line likens the fates (al-manāyā) to the random trampling of such a night-blind she-camel
(shāhid: al-Ḥuṭayʾa, on coming to a generous man's fire)
its words do not follow analogy and cannot be reduced to one underlying meaning
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: the root has no one underlying meaning

highlights.text: عَذُبَ الْمَاءُ (ʿaḏuba, verbal noun ʿuḏūba) = the water became sweet/pleasant; the adjective is عَذْب (ʿaḏb, "sweet")
Torment / punishment (al-ʿaḏāb). The verb is عَذَّبَ (ʿaḏḏaba, "to torment")
citing Zuhayr (a beast that "when she fears the ʿaḏāb [the beating] stretches out her back and neck")
a ḥadīth, "Refrain (aʿḏibū) from the mention of women,"
the root ʿ-dh-r has many branches but no single unifying meaning — each cluster stands on its own
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: no single unifying meaning

highlights.text: a person's attempt, by speech, to set right something for which he has been blamed
Verb of apologizing: iʿtadhara ("he made excuse for his sin"); noun al-maʿdhira.
"qālū maʿdhiratan ilā rabbikum" — "as an excuse before your Lord" (7:164)
ʿadhdhara (form II) = to make a show of exerting oneself while actually slacking
Shāhid from Imruʾ al-Qays: she "proved hard against me and swore an unbreakable oath."
Ḥadīth: "the Jews are the foulest of creatures in ʿadhira," i.e. in their courtyard
highlights.note: a hadith, giving ʿadhira the sense "forecourt"

highlights.text: one sound root: holding on to a thing with the teeth
The primary use is biting with the teeth: ʿaḍiḍtu, aʿaḍḍu ("I bit, I bite")
Al-Aṣmaʿī's proverb, "You are like one who turns back to the one who bites"
al-Aʿshā describes choice white camels "hardened by ʿuḍḍ, by grazing the reserved pasture, and by long barrenness"
a sound root pointing to a bodily organ, and that this is then used metaphorically for strength and for a helper/supporter
Al-ʿaḍud is the upper arm (elbow to shoulder)
By metaphor, al-ʿaḍd means help/support — "ʿaḍadtu fulānan" = "I supported him."
highlights.note: عَضُد in the sense of support (Q 28:35)

highlights.text: The entry cites Qur'an 18:51, "Nor was I to take the misleaders as a supporter [ʿaḍudan],"
A weak or unhelpful person could be mocked as "the chipped ʿaḍud" (a Bedouin saying quoted here)
Al-ʿaḍad (different vowel) names a disease of the upper arm/foreleg, illustrated with a verse of al-Nābigha
A ḥadīth about Medina is quoted: "its trees are not to be cut [lā yuʿḍad]."
one core idea: intensity/hardship combined with twistedness — something that resists being straightened out or resolved
ʿAḍaltu l-marʾata / ʿaḍḍaltuhā — to unjustly bar a woman from marrying
glossing ʿaḍl here as taḥbis — "restrain/confine,"
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's gloss of ʿaḍl in Q 2:232

highlights.text: Illustrated by a verse attributed to Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ, who couldn't get his people to pay one wife's dowry
illustrated with a line of poetry by Aws describing a plain "sickened" and "constricted" by a huge host.
ʿUmar's remark that the people of Kufa had worn him out (aʿḍala bī)
a single idea runs through this root — dividing a thing into parts
"those who made the Qur'an ʿiḍīn." Al-Khalīl explains ʿiḍīn as "portion by portion" — they split the Qur'an up
"the religion of God is not something fragmented" (بِالْمُعَضَّى)
highlights.note: Ruʾba, Umayyad; the entry names no earlier poet

highlights.text: "there is no taʿḍiya in an inheritance" — meaning one must not divide up an inheritance item that cannot bear division without ruining its value, giving a sword or a pearl as examples.
highlights.note: a hadith, on dividing an inheritance

highlights.text: one sound root whose single idea is BINDING one thing to another — either lengthwise or by wrapping round
Al-ʿuṣba per al-Khalīl is ten men, and nothing fewer is called that; it is so named because it is "bound," as if tied one to another
ʿUṣba and ʿiṣāba are used of people, birds and horses
al-Nābigha: bands of birds circling over armies, guided by other bands
يوم عصيب / يوم عصبصب, a hard day
Ḥassān — men are "people of ʿaṣb and manliness."
those who inherit by kalāla, without parent or child; in the fixed-share system, anyone whose share is not named is ʿaṣaba and takes what remains after the fixed shares
a single sound root whose core notion is lightness and speed
ʿaṣf — chaff and dry plant matter. The husk of straw on the grain
ʿāṣif — a violent, sweeping wind. Cited from Q 10:22, "a ʿāṣif wind came upon them,"
"sweeps away" a people, as in al-Aʿshā's line about a dense army that carries off armoured and unarmoured men alike
some commentators explain ʿaṣf as any crop whose grain has been eaten and whose straw is left
highlights.note: commentators' reading of ʿaṣf in Q 105:5

highlights.text: one sound root with a single core idea in three shades: holding back, preventing/withholding, and clinging/adhering
iʿtaṣama bi-llāh = he shielded himself [by holding to God]; istaʿṣama = he sought refuge.
aʿṣamtu fulānan = I gave someone a handhold to cling to.
al-ʿiṣma also = anything you hold fast to
Shāhid: al-Nābigha — the frightened sailor clings to the rudder-pole in dread and thunder.
three separate sound roots: (1) an age or stretch of time; (2) squeezing something until its liquid runs out; (3) clinging to something and taking hold of it for protection
ʿaṣr = time, an age (dahr). Cited from the Qur'an: "By al-ʿaṣr, man is indeed in loss" (103:1)
Imruʾ al-Qays: "Good morning to you, O worn ruin — but can one greet with good morning a man of the ages gone by?"
ʿuṣāra = what runs out of a thing you press; the same as ʿaṣīr (pressed juice)
Aws: "There is no recovery from Ḍabbāʾ while oil is still pressed."
al-muʿṣirāt = clouds that bring rain — "And We sent down from the muʿṣirāt water pouring forth" (78:14)
iʿṣār = dust rising in a circling column (whirlwind); plural aʿāṣīr
He also cites a ḥadīth in which "keep to the two ʿaṣrs" is explained as a prayer before sunrise and one before sunset
highlights.note: a hadith, on the two ʿaṣr prayers

highlights.text: "And in it they yaʿṣirūn" (12:49) was explained as "they draw produce from their lands"
its origin is resisting or holding out with one's staff
Al-ʿaṣā is a staff or stick
"So-and-so cast down his staff" means he halted and settled
A poet says: "so she cast down her staff, and her destination settled with her."
highlights.note: unattributed verse (the entry names no poet)

highlights.text: the root sense of al-ʿaṣā is gathering and concord
highlights.note: Abū ʿUbayd, quoted for the root sense

highlights.text: Defined as the opposite of obedience. ʿaṣā al-ʿabdu rabbahu: the servant disobeyed his Lord, going against His command.
Verbal nouns ʿaṣy, ʿiṣyān, maʿṣiya; the doer is ʿāṣin or ʿaṣiyy; ʿāṣāhu means the same
"Soft of staff" or "weak of staff" describes a gentle manager who rarely beats his animals, which is praise (Ibn al-Aʿrābī); verses of Maʿn ibn Aws and al-Rāʿī illustrate it
highlights.note: Maʿn ibn Aws, lived into Islam

highlights.text: "The staff is from the little staff" (al-Aṣmaʿī, on a son resembling his father)
"Do not lift your staff from your family", al-Kisāʾī and others say no literal staff or beating is meant: it is a figure for not neglecting their discipline
highlights.note: a hadith, read figuratively by al-Kisāʾī

highlights.text: "Were it not that we disobey God, He would not 'disobey' us": that is, He would not withhold His answer
highlights.note: a saying, glossing ʿiṣyān as withholding

highlights.text: Ibn Fāris states this root has one single sound sense: bending and curving
The two sides of a person are called al-ʿiṭfān because a person leans on them
the idiom thanā ʿiṭfahu, "he bent his side" — said of someone who turned away from you and treated you with coldness/disdain
a line of the poet Labīd using ʿāṭif in exactly this sense — "one who folds the cushion"
emptiness, vacancy — something left devoid or unattended
"ʿuṭṭilat al-dāru" — a house left empty, abandoned.
"an abandoned well" (Q22:45), and "when the ten-months-pregnant she-camels are left untended" (Q81:4)
a single sound meaning: taking, and handing or passing something over
ʿaṭāʾ (العَطاء) — a noun for the thing given
the sense of "giving" is derived from this root of reaching/handing
taʿāṭī (التعاطي) — a narrowed, negative use: taking or reaching for what one has no right to
Imruʾ al-Qays uses the verb taʿṭū of a woman reaching out with soft fingers
one sound root meaning largeness and strength
the verbal noun (maṣdar) of al-ʿaẓīm ("the great/mighty thing")
al-ʿaẓm — "bone," which he says belongs to this root
a coming-together under weight — things gathered up in a way that makes them heavy or bulky
the idiom mā ʿabaʾtu bihi shayʾan ("I gave it no ʿabʾ at all") means "I didn't care about it"
Cited verse: a poet speaks of "bearing the load off the necks of my people."
highlights.note: unattributed verse (the entry names no poet)

highlights.text: two sound but seemingly opposite roots: one meaning softness and lowliness, the other strength and hardness
al-ʿabd = an owned person (al-mamlūk)
common usage separates ʿibād Allāh ("servants of God") from al-ʿabīd ("owned slaves")
taʿabbada X ("he made X like a slave to himself, though X was free")
cited from Ṭarafa's line about being cast out like a tarred camel
an interpretation of Q 43:81, {…fa-anā awwalu l-ʿābidīn}, as "I am the first to be angered by / to disdain such a claim"
a saying attributed to ʿAlī, ʿabidtu fa-ṣamattu ("I was angered, so I kept silent")
anything unusually excellent or extraordinary — a person, an animal, or a piece of cloth — used to be attributed to it
highlights.note: the sense the entry gives ʿabqarī

highlights.text: ʿabqariyy denotes a kind of furnishing or carpet
the saying arose about the caliph ʿUmar: I have not seen an ʿabqarī like him
highlights.note: a report about the caliph ʿUmar

highlights.text: a single sound root whose core idea is passing through something and going on across it
عَابِر سَبِيل is one who is merely passing through
عَبَرَ الرُّؤْيَا (verbal nouns عَبْر, عِبَارَة) and عَبَّرَ (تَعْبِير) mean to explain it
اعْتِبَار and عِبْرَة (taking heed). He proposes that both come from the two facing banks of a river
al-Khalīl's definition of عِبْرَة as drawing a lesson from what has passed
Imruʾ al-Qays: "my cure is a flow of tears, if I pour it out — yet is there at an effaced camp-trace anything to lean on?"
reads Q 59:2 "So take heed, O you possessed of insight" accordingly: look at those who acted and were punished
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 59:2

highlights.text: one sound root whose core notion is aversion or repugnance toward something
al-yawm al-ʿabūs, "the scowling day," meaning a day that is harsh and repellent
the verb ʿabasa / yaʿbisu / ʿubūs — to scowl
camels were passed by that had become "ʿabasat" — crusted over in their own urine.
highlights.note: a hadith, for the concrete sense

highlights.text: one sound root with a single core meaning: mixing (al-khalṭ)
the word "al-ʿabath" came to denote an action done without evenness or soundness
glosses ʿabathan here as laʿiban ("in play/sport," i.e., without purpose).
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's gloss of ʿabathan in Q 23:115
